No correction needed, so the push only appends a dated review line to spec/asama-0/CHANGELOG.md, plus this ledger and reports/.

MF1 built: referee/ledger/chain.py (RFC 8785 with keys in UTF-16 order, integers only per tohum/26, duplicate keys/NaN/lone surrogates/deep nesting refused; row_hash = sha256(canonical(row - row_hash) || prev_hash); verify checks link, own hash, and with --previous byte-identical prefix). Test 13 = referee/tests/test_chain.py, 22 tests / 43 cases, all through the CLI in a subprocess from referee/, files via /dev/fd pipes so it runs in a read-only container. V1 -> 3bae9158..., V2 -> 3b10a5bb..., V3 -> broken r2 line 2; founder-ledger.jsonl verifies. Deliberate breakage: 12 mutants (plain code-point sort, prev_hash left out of hash, row_hash kept in body, link check off, hash check off, --previous ignored, prefix length-only, floats allowed, duplicate keys allowed, control chars unescaped, upper-case hex, recursion guard removed) each turn the suite red; deleting ledger/chain.py turns all 43 cases red. snowball-tests.json: T13, done_mf [1].

Interface choices where 29a:70-71 is silent: verify exits 0 valid, 1 broken, 2 unusable input (missing file, usage), always one JSON line {valid, broken_row, line, reason}; broken_row is the row_id or 'line:N' when the line has none; hash refuses (exit 2, {error}) more or fewer than one line, a bad prev_hash, and floats. Floats are refused rather than serialised the ECMAScript way because tohum/26:31-33 bans floating point in hashed artifacts, so a float row is a broken row. A row re-serialised with different whitespace is a valid chain but not append-only (byte prefix), because the file, not its parse, is what was published.

[seed_issue] seed-007-chain-cli-exit-and-broken-row: 29a:70-71 gives verify's output as {valid, broken_row} but not the exit code for a broken chain nor the broken_row value for a line with no row_id; 29d:92-100 says the generic runner compares the stdout JSON and treats only exit 125 as runner_fault. If the seed's runner treats exit 1 as a failed command, V3 (a correctly reported broken chain) would be red. The Founder's chain exits 1 on a broken chain and names such lines 'line:N'.

Interface choices where 26a, 29a and 29d are silent: python -m gate.secrets scan --kind diff|row|prompt [--known-env NAME] [FILE|stdin] prints {clean, kind, run_valid, matches}; send [--known-env NAME] -- CMD runs CMD with the prompt on stdin only when it is clean and prints {clean, run_valid, sent, sender_exit, matches}; exit 0 clean, 1 match, 2 unusable input (never clean). A match is {rule, line, sha256[, path]}: no value, per 30c:10-11. Each line is scanned raw, with \uXXXX/\xNN decoded, and NFKC-folded without format characters; a whole diff is scanned, removed lines included, since a diff in a prompt leaks either way. Library: scan, require_clean (raises SecretFound), send_if_clean, for llm.call, gate.check and ledger.append later.

gate/secrets.py: the assignment value is no longer captured by a character class but read by _value: unquoted, it runs to the first whitespace outside brackets (one trailing , ; . : and unmatched closers are syntax); quoted, to the closing quote not escaped by a backslash, with an optional string prefix (f, b, r) and a glued tail. A value is skipped only when it is nothing but templates, one repeated character, a placeholder word, or (unquoted) code by an explicit recursive-descent grammar (_is_code: dotted or underscored letter names, or calls, subscripts, slices and groups over names, numbers and string literals). Same class, found by me while fixing and closed in this push: a subscripted key (config[name] = value), comparisons (== != === !==), type annotations and the Go string type, command-line flags followed by a value, an Authorization scheme word before an opaque token, an escaped quote inside a quoted value, text glued after a closing quote, and a URL password shorter than 6 characters. The two-line join for assignments now only gives a key that ends a line its value from the next line (the old join glued unrelated lines into fake annotations). Three structure choices for MF7. (1) One source for the 29f rules: coverage as written and agent configuration as written were private to profile/unit_verify.py (MF6); I moved them to profile/derive.py (MF4) as covers_as_written and agent_config_as_written, and MF6 and MF7 both call them. The derivation's own folded covers stays separate on purpose: 29f coverage is case-sensitive and as written, the derivation's is folded and normalised; merging them would change one of two specified behaviours. (2) The diff parser fails closed instead of reading only diff --git headers: git apply also applies a traditional patch with no diff --git line and ignores text before the first block, so a lenient parser could pass a diff whose real change it never saw. (3) The config lists are one table per reason in diffguard.py, seed rows and measured rows kept apart and named, so the next measurement adds a row, not a branch; the seed rows stay exactly 29g's lists so that every 29g vector keeps its meaning.

MF9 structure. (1) A pure guard in front of an injected transport: every request passes Guard.check(method, path, body) before it is sent, and a refused request is never sent; the writer's operations (branch, fast-forward update, commit, pull request, check, merge, revert) are thin calls through it. One rule set then judges the writer, the vectors (python -m target.write guard PLAN) and any later caller (MF10 ledger.append, MF13 gate.revert, MF18 activate), instead of a check per operation. (2) A closed route list, not a deny list: 11 routes under /repos/<owner>/<repo>/ of one repository; the contents API, the merges endpoint, ref deletion, repository settings, GraphQL and other repositories are refused because they are not listed, so a route nobody thought of is refused too. Blobs and trees are left out until their first caller (MF10, Y4). (3) Merge is guarded by what the guard saw: only a pull request seen open in a response, base and head under brain/, head sha pinned, merge_method merge (two parents, so the revert rule can read the first parent). (4) Revert: only the head of the branch, only a two-parent commit; tree = first parent's tree, one parent (the merge); it goes onto a brain/c/ branch and through a pull request, because brain/integration takes no direct push (tohum/01b), so the revert passes the gate like a candidate (tohum/07). (5) The HTTPS transport follows no redirect: urllib would carry the Authorization header and a POST turned GET to the Location host. deps_npm already does the same (_NoRedirect); I did not merge the two classes: deps_npm raises its own DepsError inside the getir job and target.write returns an ApiError in yaz, and one shared three-line class across two jobs with different error types is the wrong abstraction. (6) One way, tested structurally: no referee module except target/write.py names a github.com host or a push/send-pack command, and only target/write.py and runner/deps_npm.py import a network module; deps_npm is checked to open bare URLs only (no Request, data, method or headers).

Addendum after f127, before the push: my own MF2 scanner (python -m gate.secrets scan --kind diff on this push's staged diff) reported secret-assignment at two lines: a json.dumps call with the sort-keys keyword set to True and then .encode(...) chained on, once in target/write.py and once in tests/fake_github.py. Cause: the keyword name sort_keys is secret-named by rule (c) (a word ending in keys plus another word), and the unquoted value (the word True, a closing bracket, then the chained call) runs past the unbalanced ) because only a trailing closing bracket is syntax; the value has 8 or more characters. That is the scanner's stated cost (gate/secrets.py comment at NAME_PARTS: code after a secret-named key is reported), so the rule is not changed here; stopping the value at an unbalanced closing bracket would also drop an .env password whose value holds a closing bracket, a miss I will not trade for precision without a measured false-positive rate. Code changed for its own reasons, not to pass: the HTTP body needs no key order (removed), and the fake's object id now uses ledger.chain.canonical, the one canonical JSON in referee/, instead of a second json.dumps form. Rescan: clean. T49 green again (36). Open, for a later MF2 revision with data: the false-positive rate of rule (c) plus code values on real code (keyword arguments whose name ends in _keys).

MF9 under 29i. One Writer serves both the live transport and the vector's Replay ({"METHOD /path": body}, 200 or 404), so the vectors judge the code that will write the target, not a second path. Changes the replay's fixed call list forced, each stated in the docstring: (1) merge no longer reads the base back after merging (that GET would be a 404 in replay); the merge is pinned to the head sha read from GET pulls/<n> and is done when the API says merged true with a sha. (2) A created pull request (POST pulls) is no longer a record for the guard; a merge always reads it again. (3) revert(merge, onto, ref, message) reads the merge, its first parent and onto's head (29i order), then commits {tree: first parent's tree, parents: [onto's head]} and creates ref; the pull request is the caller's next op, not part of revert. I kept revert_not_head: 29i says parents = onto's head and does not say that head is the merge; when it is not, the first parent's tree undoes later merges. I hold the safer rule and filed seed-024; if a refs vector reverts a non-head merge, the disagreement is on that rule and the report says why. (4) outputs come from what was sent (Writer.sent) and the refs the guard named for each 2xx write (Writer.written): one source, the guard. Exit 1 only for rule refusals, which happen before the first write; exit 2 reports the writes truly attempted. The duplicate pull-request ref check in the command layer was removed (the guard already refuses, before sending); the up-front ref check for branch, update and revert stays, because the branch is cut out of the ref by length and a ref like refs/tags/xbrain/c/1 would become brain/c/1 without it (a mutant showed this).

MF15 shape. dispatcher/llm_call.py has one type checker (TYPES, check_value) used for both the typed input and the structured output, and one call path: render, pin, scan, brake, one process, classify, cost row. Two choices were deliberate. (1) Values enter the prompt as their RFC 8785 form (ledger.chain.canonical, the existing canonical writer, not a second one): a string arrives quoted and escaped, so a value cannot close its quotes, add a line or expand another placeholder. (2) A field outside the type is refused, not dropped: the vector's changed input must not give the expected sha256, and a dropped field would give the same sha, so the vector could not tell whether the field got in. The cost row is recorded into a CostBook for every started process, before call returns, and the book's request() is the cycle's ledger.append input, so there is one brain/state commit per cycle (MF10's rule), not one per call, and the brake counts this cycle's earlier calls as well as the ledger.

Classification rules for the CLI's result: timeout is outage with the cap as cost (tohum/06); an unreadable result is unresolved with the cap as cost (fail closed: an unknown cost is the most it could have been); 429/401/403/5xx outage, 400/404/413/422 request_rejected (tohum/24, 29b); a network error without a status is cli_error (unresolved). That last one disagrees with tohum/24, which counts network errors as outages, but I found no stable form of the CLI's network error to recognise. Classing it as unresolved never accepts a bad run; it can make a real outage look like a failed run. This is open in seed-033 (e). No retry inside a call: a test counts one process for a 429.

Root cause, not the instance: the cost was computed by decimal arithmetic, and every decimal context has a precision and exponent limits. The same class held four more defects the rival did not show, all reproduced before the fix: (1) 1e99999999999999999999 raised decimal.InvalidOperation inside json.loads (an ArithmeticError, not a ValueError, so classify's except did not catch it: another crash after a started process); (2) 1e-9999999 underflowed to 0 and the ceiling gave 0 micro for a positive cost (must be 1); (3) a mantissa longer than 28 digits was rounded half-even before the ceiling, 0.0000010000000000000000000000000001 gave 1 micro, not 2; (4) a 5000-digit integer anywhere hit Python's int-string limit. Rejected alternatives: catching decimal.Overflow (hides the class, keeps (2)-(4)); a local context with MAX_PREC/MAX_EMAX (still a context, still a limit at 10^999999999999999999, memory with huge operands). Chosen: no decimal at all. _strict_json keeps every fraction/exponent number, and every integer of more than 18 digits, as JsonNumber(text) (neither int nor str, so no type check takes it); to_micros(text) computes the exact ceiling in micro-USD by integer arithmetic on the digit string, with a magnitude pre-check (leading digit at 10^16 or above -> None) and an exponent of more than 18 digits decided by its sign alone, so work is bounded by the text's length whatever the exponent. One reader for every JSON number in the result; classify's cost step is total over JSON numbers.

Design, each choice with its reason. (1) One converter, runner/lint_record.py: ESLint --format json stdout plus the worktree it read -> gate.check's run record {tool, violations: [{rule_id, path, line, fix}]}; run_file writes base.jsonl/cand.jsonl next to check.run_file's reader, so the run file shape has one writer and one reader. (2) Its caller is MF6 (unit.verify step 6, criteria 4 and 5), not MF7 or MF8: the calls order requires a called MF to come before its caller, so criterion 5 uses MF4's coverage (security_paths, excluded_dirs, excluded_paths, inside inputs) and states that config, manifest and lock files still count (MF7's rule not called). (3) Lines are git lines, not ESLint's: measured with real ESLint 10.13.0, ESLint counts a lone CR and U+2028/2029 as line breaks and gives columns and fix ranges in UTF-16 units of the text without its BOM; the converter maps every position to an offset and counts only LF, so the gate's mapped line and scope rule see the same lines as the diff. (4) Suppressed messages are violations (gate/check.py's own note): measured end to end, a real eslint-disable-next-line candidate is not_distinguished with them and merges without them. (5) A parse error (ruleId null, fatal) refuses the run: its file's violations vanish, which would lower the ratchet count. (6) A non-fatal message with no rule id (unused directive) gets the reserved id eslint:no-rule-id. (7) fix range: first = line of the start; last = line of the last replaced unit, or the next line when that unit is LF and the new text does not end with LF (the next line is joined).

Design (one source): class Marks reads the request against one lock and is used by all three paths (the npmlock vector 'fetch', the production 'store' and the static 'check' unit.verify calls). A mark is a key of this lock's packages other than '' or name@version with an npm name (NAME_RE, scoped allowed) and a semver version (VERSION_RE); every other element lands in bad. Before, the vector path matched name@version only and the production path had its own _marked; the two now cannot drift. Choices: (1) a range or tag after @ (left-pad@^1.0, left-pad@latest) is not a mark: 26c's sürüm is a version, and a range would mark several versions, the class 26c refuses for bare names. (2) For 'check' (static, used by unit.verify) a non-mark is the reason mark_not_usable:<element>, so a recipe with one is refused with its reason (lock:mark_not_usable:x); for 'store' and 'fetch' (deps.fetch) it is exit 2 before any tarball is read, as 26c says. (3) Every exit 2 line now carries ok false beside error (29g: {"ok": false}, free error), for all subcommands, not only fetch.

Fix: one process boundary, referee/cli.py, and every __main__ block is exactly sys.exit(cli.run(main, sys.argv[1:], FAULT_LINE)). run holds main's stdout and writes it only after main returned an int 0, 1 or 2; an Exception or SystemExit inside main, a bad return (True, None, 3) or a stdout that fails is exit 2, stderr 'internal error: <type>' (never the message: it can carry scanned text, 30c), stdout the module's fault line, then fd 1 to /dev/null so shutdown cannot make 120. Design of D1's accepted-SHA check, one source per rule. (1) loop.treehash is the one implementation of 26c's referee_tree_sha256: one core over (path, kind, bytes) entries with two adapters, a tar (the page's known answer) and a commit read by loop.gitobj (the brain as committed, no checkout attributes); OPERATOR_NAMES is the one copy of 25a item 1's list (no earlier copy existed in the brain). (2) loop.accepted holds 29b's read: choose (newest unexpired bootstrap-state of a main run of the repository itself, listing order not trusted, a malformed entry stops the read rather than being skipped, since a skipped entry could be the newest), unpack (exactly the two files), the exact sigstore verify identity argv, and the parse of state.last_accepted_sha only after the verifier passed; plus last_import (ledger.chain.verify_bytes reused, no second chain reader) and check_tree. Its HTTP reader is not target.write.HttpTransport: the artifact zip is a 302 to another host and the token must not follow it, so a redirect handler captures the location and the blob is fetched bare. (3) job.cek_d1 composes them; unusable reads exit 2 (29b: the reader stops), a hash mismatch or a broken import is a refusal (exit 1); the job still ends cycle_not_wired. (4) Three registers changed by the wiring, each kept rather than bypassed: my workflow rule secret_outside now lets cek hold github.token only (D1's Actions read needs the job's own read token; 29p and test 46 do not forbid it, my rule was stricter); MF9's OneWay now names loop.accepted as a GET-only network reader with a test that it builds bare Requests; the hand-over register gained a status 'unwritten' (a named test runs the producer to cycle_not_wired and no call writes the artifact) for the four pulled edges, with proofs that it fails for a producer that writes and for a test that never runs it. Architecture: the Cargo rule follows Cargo's own resolution, in one place (status.depmap): a project is every Cargo.toml below the root with a [package] table (the same rule as pyproject.toml, a virtual manifest is none); cargo_workspace(d) finds the package's workspace root as Cargo does (package.workspace, else its own [workspace], else the nearest one above unless its exclude holds it, by path segments, not text); cargo_dep_paths resolves each dependency through that root: its path, a workspace = true entry's path from the root, or the root's [patch.crates-io] for a crates.io dependency (by the crate's name, a rename's package included). Kept: those handlers (they also guard values not parsed here); secrets' 'a row nests too deep to scan' is now unreachable from JSON input. Why 128: deepest measured JSON is 6 in /vec and 10 in the target's 1190 JSON files; 128 levels leave room for walks of up to 7 frames a level.
